opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, that's kind of the whole point. The way we think about it, if a robot gets lost doing a dangerous job, that's a robot that went instead of a person. You'd much rather lose a machine than a soldier. That's the fundamental trade, and in Ukraine you see it every day.

The economics have shifted a lot too. Ground robots and drones are now cheap enough that they're treated almost like consumables. Look at FPV drones: they're built to be used once. Ground systems are heading the same way for things like casualty evacuation, resupply to forward positions, laying or clearing mines, or just being the first thing through a door or across an open field. Those are exactly the tasks where a human is most exposed, so they're exactly where you want to accept attrition.

So when we design or invest, we ask a few questions. Is the platform cheap enough to lose without it hurting? Can it be produced at scale, quickly, from components that aren't a single point of failure in the supply chain? And can it keep working when GPS and comms are jammed, because electronic warfare is brutal there? A robot that's too expensive to risk ends up sitting in the rear, and then it isn't doing anything useful.

The other thing Ukraine has taught everyone is how fast the cycle moves. Something that works this month may be countered in six or eight weeks. So you don't want a beautiful, exquisite system you're afraid to lose. You want something good enough, affordable, and quick to iterate. You accept that you'll lose a lot of them, you learn from every loss, and you push the next version out fast.

So the risk of losing robots isn't really a risk to manage away. It's something you plan for. The goal is to make losing them economically and operationally fine, because every one lost in an exposed task is potentially a life saved.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exposed tasks and crossing open fields, but does not identify drone attacks when soldiers leave strongholds as a central danger.

r002.rationale: It says losing a robot means it went instead of a person, and that losing a machine is preferable to losing a soldier on dangerous tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the way I think about it is that losing the robot is the point. That's the whole value proposition. When we send a ground robot forward to do something like carry supplies to a trench line, pull a wounded soldier back, or go clear a route we think is mined, the question we're really answering is: do I want to risk a machine here, or do I want to risk a person? And every time, if the machine can do the job even reasonably well, the machine should go.

So I don't frame it as a loss in the way you'd think about losing an expensive piece of equipment. I frame it as a trade. If a system that costs tens of thousands of dollars gets destroyed and a nineteen-year-old comes home, that's not a failure. That's the system doing exactly what it was built to do.

That said, it does force a couple of design decisions. The first is cost. If you're building something you expect to lose, it has to be cheap enough and simple enough that losing it doesn't hurt. You can't put a half-million-dollar sensor suite on a platform that's going to drive into a minefield on purpose. That means a lot of the engineering is about figuring out what's good enough rather than what's best. The Ukrainians have been incredibly disciplined about this. They'll take a commercial platform, strip it down, bolt on what they actually need, and accept that it has a short life expectancy.

The second thing is what happens to the robot when it's captured or recovered by the other side. You have to assume anything you send forward can end up in enemy hands. So you design for that. You don't put sensitive software or communications on something that's going to be sitting in no-man's-land. You think about how quickly the other side can reverse engineer it, and you assume they will. In practice that pushes you toward systems that are more disposable and less clever, which is a hard mindset shift for a lot of defense engineers who've spent their careers building exquisite platforms.

And the third thing, which I think people underestimate, is the human side. Operators get attached to these things. We've seen it going back to the early EOD robots in Iraq and Afghanistan, where soldiers would hold funerals for a robot that got blown up. Part of that is a joke, but part of it is real. So you have to train teams to see the robot as a tool you expect to spend, not a teammate you're trying to keep alive. If an operator hesitates to send the robot forward because they don't want to lose it, you've defeated the purpose.

So the short answer is: I worry much less about losing robots than I worry about not losing enough of them. If the robots are all coming back intact, it probably means we're still sending people to do the jobs the robots should be doing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots doing exposed tasks but does not identify drone attacks when soldiers leave their strongholds as a central danger.

r002.rationale: It explicitly argues that a robot should take the risk instead of a person, and that losing a robot can be an acceptable trade if a soldier comes home.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to compare losing a robot with losing the person who would otherwise be doing that job. If you send a robot out on an exposed task and it gets destroyed, you’ve lost equipment. That matters—you want it to be reliable and affordable to replace—but you haven’t lost a human life.

You also have to ask whether it accomplished anything. Did it get supplies where they needed to go? Did it give you information that kept someone else out of danger? You don’t want to throw robots away pointlessly, but bringing every robot home can’t be the measure of success. The point is to reduce the risk to people.

r001.rationale: It discusses exposed tasks and robot destruction, but does not identify drone attacks or soldiers leaving strongholds as the central danger.

r002.rationale: It explicitly contrasts losing a robot with losing a person and says the goal is reducing risk to people.

sol-6.1.text: I think you have to compare that risk with the alternative. If you send a robot out to do an exposed task and lose it, that’s a piece of equipment you have to replace. If you send a person and lose them, you can’t replace that life. That doesn’t mean you’re careless with the robots. You want them to be reliable, useful, and affordable enough that losing one doesn’t make the mission unsustainable. But protecting people is the point. If a robot takes on that risk so a soldier doesn’t have to, it’s doing its job.
